question: In Britain and its colonies, the day after 2 September 1752 was officially 14 September 1752. Why did eleven days simply disappear from the calendar?
correct_answer: Switch from Julian to Gregorian calendar
alternative_answers: Calendar reform to the Gregorian system
Correcting the Julian calendar's drift against the solar year
Britain caught up with the Gregorian calendar used in Europe
headline_answer: Switch from Julian to Gregorian calendar
source_excerpt: The Act advanced the calendar date by 11 days to realign with the solar year, with 2 September 1752 being followed by 14 September 1752.

extra.verification_notes: The Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 switched Britain and colonies from Julian to Gregorian calendar, skipping 11 days from 2-14 September 1752 to correct accumulated drift.

explanation: Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar with the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750, catching up with most of Catholic Europe, which had switched back in 1582. The older Julian calendar counted every fourth year as a leap year without exception, so it drifted about three days every four centuries against the solar year. By 1752 the gap had grown to eleven days, so Parliament ordered them dropped in one jump: people went to bed on 2 September and woke up on 14 September. The same act also moved the start of the legal year from 25 March to 1 January.

question: Which Greek philosopher was hired by King Philip of Macedon to tutor his teenage son, the future Alexander the Great?
source_excerpt: In 343 BCE, King Philip II of Macedon hired Aristotle to educate his thirteen-year-old son, Alexander.

extra.why_interesting: Players know both names but rarely connect them; the greatest philosopher of antiquity spent years as a schoolteacher to the future conqueror of Persia.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm Philip II of Macedon hired Aristotle in 343 BCE to tutor the teenage Alexander.

explanation: Aristotle taught Alexander for about three years from the age of thirteen, and Aristotle had himself been a pupil of Plato, so the chain runs Socrates to Plato to Aristotle to Alexander.

question: How many years did Nelson Mandela spend in prison before his release in 1990?
source_excerpt: Nelson Mandela ... was released from prison after 27 years on February 11, 1990.

extra.why_interesting: Most players know it was 'a very long time'; the exact figure, and the fact he became president only four years later, makes the number land.
extra.verification_notes: Mandela was released on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison, a well-documented and undisputed historical fact.

explanation: He was jailed in 1962 and spent most of those years on Robben Island, then walked out in 1990 and was elected president of South Africa just four years later.

question: Marie Curie is the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Which two?
source_excerpt: Marie Curie is the only person to have won a Nobel Prize in two different sciences, physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

extra.why_interesting: Players know she won twice; naming the two fields makes them realise she was not simply 'the radioactivity scientist' but crossed disciplines.
extra.verification_notes: Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911); no one has repeated this since.

explanation: She shared the 1903 Physics prize for research on radioactivity, then won the 1911 Chemistry prize on her own for discovering polonium and radium.

question: Which British prime minister won the Nobel Prize in Literature?
source_excerpt: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1953 was awarded to Winston Churchill "for his mastery of historical and biographical description..."

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a wartime leader would get a Peace Prize if anything; the Literature prize for a sitting prime minister is the surprise.
extra.verification_notes: Winston Churchill, who served as British Prime Minister, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 for his historical/biographical writing and oratory.

explanation: He won it in 1953 for his historical writing and speeches, while he was serving his second term in Downing Street.

question: Which scientist, famous for his laws of motion, spent the last three decades of his life running England's Royal Mint and personally hunting down counterfeiters?
source_excerpt: Isaac Newton, Warden and Master of the Royal Mint 1696-1727

extra.why_interesting: The stern figure of gravity and calculus is hard to picture as a detective prowling London taverns, yet that is how he spent his final decades.
extra.verification_notes: Newton served as Warden (1696) then Master (1699) of the Royal Mint until his death in 1727 — roughly the last three decades of his life — and personally investigated/prosecuted counterfeiters like William Chaloner.

explanation: Newton became Warden of the Mint in 1696, went undercover in taverns to gather evidence, and sent the notorious forger William Chaloner to the gallows.

question: In 1952, which world-famous physicist was offered the presidency of Israel and politely turned it down?
source_excerpt: he had neither the natural ability nor the experience to deal properly with people and to exercise official functions

extra.why_interesting: Players think of Einstein as purely a scientist; the idea that he could have been a head of state, and turned it down, is a genuine jolt.
extra.verification_notes: Confirmed: after President Chaim Weizmann's death in 1952, Einstein was offered Israel's presidency and declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience.

explanation: The offer came from Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion after the first president died, and Einstein replied that he lacked the aptitude for dealing with people and official functions.

question: Mansa Musa, often called the richest man who ever lived, ruled which West African empire in the fourteenth century?
source_excerpt: Mansa Musa was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire, which reached its territorial peak during his reign.

extra.why_interesting: Players may have heard 'richest man ever' but usually cannot place him on the map; the answer relocates medieval wealth away from Europe.
extra.verification_notes: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire c. 1312–1337, matching the question and answer.

explanation: His 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca gave away so much gold along the way that the metal's price in Cairo reportedly slumped for years afterwards.

question: Which future Roman leader, kidnapped by pirates as a young man, reportedly complained that his ransom was set too low, then had his captors crucified once he was freed?
source_excerpt: he laughed at them for not knowing who it was they had captured and suggested that 50 talents would be a more appropriate amount

extra.why_interesting: The audacity of demanding a higher ransom for yourself is so on-brand that players who hear the story can deduce the man from the personality.
extra.verification_notes: Well-documented anecdote confirmed by Plutarch and modern historians: Caesar insisted his pirate captors raise the ransom from 20 to 50 talents, then after release raised a fleet and had them crucified.

explanation: Plutarch says the pirates asked for twenty talents and Caesar insisted on fifty, then raised ships after his release, captured the pirates and had them executed as he had promised.

question: The video-game company Nintendo was founded in which decade?
source_excerpt: Nintendo was founded on September 23, 1889

extra.why_interesting: Players anchor Nintendo to the 1980s console boom; learning it predates the automobile age reframes the company entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Nintendo was founded on September 23, 1889 in Kyoto (as a playing-card company, later becoming a video-game company), confirming the 1880s answer.

explanation: Nintendo started in Kyoto in 1889 making hanafuda playing cards, and did not release a video game until roughly eighty years later.

question: True or false: Christopher Columbus set foot on the mainland of what is now the United States.
source_excerpt: Columbus never set foot on the mainland of North America, let alone the United States.

extra.why_interesting: The 'Columbus discovered America' shorthand makes most players assume he landed in what is now the USA; he never did.
extra.verification_notes: Columbus's four voyages reached the Caribbean, Central America, and Venezuela's coast, but he never set foot on the North American mainland now part of the US.

explanation: Across four voyages he landed in the Bahamas, the Caribbean islands and the coasts of Central and South America, but never the North American mainland.

question: Which former US president, campaigning for a return to office in 1912, was shot in the chest in Milwaukee and insisted on delivering his speech before going to hospital?
source_excerpt: Roosevelt insisted on delivering his scheduled speech ... before allowing himself to be taken to the hospital

extra.why_interesting: Players know him as the rugged Rough Rider; the stem's footholds of 1912 and 'former president running again' let a thoughtful player reach him.
extra.verification_notes: Confirmed: Theodore Roosevelt, running for president again in 1912 after previously serving 1901–1909, was shot in Milwaukee on Oct 14, 1912, and delivered his speech before seeking medical care.

explanation: The bullet was slowed by his folded fifty-page speech and a steel glasses case in his pocket, and he spoke for about ninety minutes with blood spreading across his shirt.

question: France last used the guillotine to execute a prisoner in which year?
source_excerpt: Djandoubi was the last person to be executed by guillotine, both in France and in the Western world.

extra.why_interesting: Players file the guillotine under the French Revolution; discovering it was still in use in the era of Star Wars and punk rock is a shock.
extra.verification_notes: Hamida Djandoubi was guillotined on 10 September 1977 in Marseille, the last execution by guillotine in France, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Hamida Djandoubi was guillotined in Marseille in September 1977, the same year Star Wars came out, and France abolished the death penalty four years later.

question: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address came straight after a two-hour oration by Edward Everett. Roughly how long did Lincoln's own speech take to deliver?
source_excerpt: Lincoln's address, some 273 words in length, was over in a couple of minutes.

extra.why_interesting: The most famous speech in American history is assumed to be a lengthy address; the two-hour opener in the stem gives a foothold to guess how tiny it really was.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm Lincoln's speech lasted roughly two to three minutes, and Everett himself famously wrote he wished he'd come as near the 'central idea' in two hours as Lincoln did in two minutes.

explanation: The address is only around 270 words long, and by some accounts the photographer had not finished setting up before Lincoln sat back down.

question: Astronauts who spend months on the International Space Station come home measurably taller than when they launched, yet shrink back to normal within days. What is happening inside their bodies?
correct_answer: Spinal discs expand without gravity's compression
alternative_answers: The spine stretches because there is no gravity
Vertebrae are no longer squeezed together
Discs between the vertebrae swell and lengthen the spine
The spine straightens out in microgravity
Gravity normally compresses the spine; in space it decompresses
headline_answer: Spinal discs expand without gravity's compression
source_excerpt: when the spine is not exposed to the pull of Earth's gravity, the vertebra can expand and relax, allowing astronauts to actually grow taller

extra.verification_notes: Scientific American confirms spinal discs/vertebrae expand without gravity's compression, adding up to ~2 inches, and compress back to normal within days to months of return to Earth.

explanation: On Earth, gravity constantly presses down on the spine and squeezes the soft discs between the vertebrae. In microgravity that load disappears, so the discs swell with fluid and the natural curves of the spine straighten, adding roughly 3 percent to an astronaut's height, often 5 centimetres or more. Back on the ground, gravity compresses the discs again and the extra height vanishes within a few days. The same effect happens in miniature every night: people are slightly taller in the morning after lying flat than in the evening after a day upright.

question: More than half of the 206 bones in an adult human are packed into just two paired body parts. Which two?
source_excerpt: 27 bones in each hand and 26 bones in each foot

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the skeleton as spine, ribs and long limb bones; the majority is actually in the small, fiddly extremities.
extra.verification_notes: Hands (27 bones × 2 = 54) and feet (26 bones × 2 = 52) total 106 of 206 bones, just over half, matching standard anatomy references.

explanation: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26, so together they account for 106 of the 206, more than the rest of the body combined.

question: Every year the Moon drifts about 4 centimetres further from Earth, almost exactly the rate at which which part of your body grows?
source_excerpt: the Moon is drifting away from Earth at 3.8 centimeters per year, about the rate your fingernails grow

extra.why_interesting: A cosmic drift sounds vast and abstract until it is pinned to something the player can see on their own hand.
extra.verification_notes: NASA and multiple sources confirm the Moon recedes ~3.8 cm/year, a rate consistently and widely compared to human fingernail growth.

explanation: Laser reflectors left by the Apollo astronauts show the Moon receding by about 3.8 centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

question: By mass, roughly two thirds of your body is a single chemical element. Which one?

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for carbon, the element of life, or hydrogen, the most common atom; the mass answer is the heavy half of water.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's elemental composition table lists oxygen at 65.0% of human body mass, consistent with 'roughly two thirds'.

explanation: Your body is mostly water, and oxygen is the heavy part of every water molecule, so oxygen makes up about 65 percent of you by mass.

question: Which part of the human body contains no blood vessels and takes its oxygen straight from the air?
source_excerpt: As an avascular surface, the primary source of oxygen for the cornea comes from the atmosphere.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every living tissue is fed by blood; one transparent part of the body breathes on its own.
extra.verification_notes: The cornea is universally recognized as the only completely avascular tissue in the human body, receiving oxygen primarily via diffusion from the atmosphere through the tear film.

explanation: The cornea must stay perfectly clear to let light in, so it has no blood vessels and absorbs oxygen from the air through the tear film.

question: Which chemical element was first detected in sunlight in 1868, nearly three decades before anyone found it on Earth?
source_excerpt: In 1895, Ramsay isolated helium on Earth ... the gas had first been detected in the spectrum of the Sun in 1868

extra.why_interesting: Players assume elements are found in the lab first; this one was found 150 million kilometres away before anyone held it, and its name is the foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Helium was detected spectroscopically in the Sun on Aug 18, 1868 by Janssen/Lockyer, and isolated on Earth by William Ramsay in 1895, a gap of ~27 years matching 'nearly three decades'.

explanation: Astronomers spotted an unknown yellow line in the Sun's spectrum and named the element after Helios, the Greek sun god, 27 years before it was found on Earth in 1895.

question: True or false: since its discovery in 1930, Pluto has completed at least one full orbit around the Sun.
source_excerpt: Pluto...won't complete its first orbit since its 1930 discovery until 2178

extra.why_interesting: Nearly a century of observation feels like plenty of time; Pluto has not even finished one lap.
extra.verification_notes: Pluto's orbital period is ~248 years; discovered in 1930, it will not complete a full orbit until March 2178, so 'False' is correct.

explanation: Pluto takes about 248 years to go around the Sun once, so it will not finish its first orbit since discovery until the year 2178.

question: Which planet is so light for its size that it would float if you could find a bathtub big enough?
source_excerpt: Saturn has the lowest density of any planet, 0.7 g/cc, which is less than that of water.

extra.why_interesting: A giant planet sounds heavy; the second largest one is lighter than water for its size.
extra.verification_notes: Saturn's average density (0.687 g/cm³) is the only one among solar system planets that is less than water's, making it the sole planet that would float in a hypothetically large enough bathtub.

explanation: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, with an average density of only about 0.7 grams per cubic centimetre, lower than water.

question: The smallest bone in the human body is shaped like a tiny stirrup. In which part of the body is it found?
source_excerpt: The stapes or stirrup is a bone in the middle ear... It is the smallest and lightest bone in the human body.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the biggest bone is in the leg; the tiniest sits somewhere they never think of as bony.
extra.verification_notes: The stapes, the smallest bone in the human body, is stirrup-shaped and located in the middle ear, confirming the claimed answer.

explanation: The stapes in the middle ear is only about 3 millimetres long and passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

question: Voyager 1, the first human-made object to reach interstellar space, was launched in which year?
source_excerpt: Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and is the most distant human-made object in space

extra.why_interesting: A probe still sending data today feels modern; it left Earth the same year Star Wars came out.
extra.verification_notes: Voyager 1 launched September 5, 1977 and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space in 2012, confirming the claimed answer.

explanation: Voyager 1 left Earth in September 1977 and is still transmitting more than 24 billion kilometres away, the most distant human-made object.

question: Which type of human cell has no nucleus, leaving more room for the protein that carries oxygen?
source_excerpt: In humans, as in all mammals, the mature red blood cell lacks a nucleus... allows the cell more room to store hemoglobin

extra.why_interesting: School biology teaches that every cell has a nucleus; the most numerous cell in the body throws its own away.
extra.verification_notes: Mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus, providing more space for hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein, per NCBI.

explanation: Red blood cells eject their nucleus as they mature, packing the space with haemoglobin, and they cannot divide or repair themselves as a result.

question: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
source_excerpt: Tooth enamel... is the hardest substance in the human body.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for bone as the body's hardest material; the answer is a thin coating in the mouth.
extra.verification_notes: Tooth enamel, being ~96% hydroxyapatite mineral, is universally confirmed as the hardest substance in the human body by Wikipedia and Cleveland Clinic.

explanation: Enamel is about 96 percent mineral and harder than bone, yet unlike bone it cannot regrow once it is worn away.

question: Which planet spins so slowly that one full rotation takes longer than its entire trip around the Sun?
source_excerpt: Venus spins so slowly that one rotation takes longer than its entire year. A Venusian day is about 243 Earth days, while a Venusian year lasts about 225

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a day is always a tiny slice of a year; on one planet the two are flipped, and the foothold of a slow, backwards spin gives a reasoning path.
extra.verification_notes: Venus's rotation period (~243 Earth days) exceeds its orbital period (~225 Earth days), confirmed by multiple authoritative sources.

explanation: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to turn once but only around 225 to orbit the Sun, and it even spins backwards compared with most planets.

question: Over an average lifetime, roughly how many times does a human heart beat?
source_excerpt: scientists estimate around 2.57 billion heartbeats in 70 years, 2.94 billion in 80 years, and 3.31 billion in 90 years

extra.why_interesting: Most people picture 'millions' and stop; multiplying about 70 beats a minute through a lifetime lands in the billions, which players can actually estimate on the spot.
extra.verification_notes: At ~60-100 bpm over a 70-90 year lifespan, the heart beats roughly 2.5-3.3 billion times, matching the 'Billions' option.

explanation: At around 70 beats a minute, the heart clocks up about 100,000 beats a day and close to 3 billion across an 80-year life.

question: Astronauts looking at the Sun from orbit, above Earth's atmosphere, see it as what colour?
source_excerpt: seen from space without an atmosphere filtering its light, the sun is actually white

extra.why_interesting: Every child draws the Sun yellow and most adults never question it, but astronauts consistently describe it as blindingly white — the yellow is an atmospheric illusion, not a property of the star.
extra.verification_notes: Astronomical consensus confirms the Sun appears white from space/orbit since there is no atmosphere to scatter blue wavelengths, as documented by ISS and Apollo astronauts.

explanation: The Sun radiates all visible wavelengths roughly equally, which our eyes read as white. Down on the ground, the atmosphere scatters away some of the blue light, leaving the yellowish tint we grew up drawing.

question: At the Paris 2024 Olympics, swimmers called the pool 'slow' and surprisingly few world records fell. It was the standard length and temperature, but only about 2.15 metres deep instead of the usual 3 metres. Why would a shallower pool make swimmers slower?
correct_answer: Waves bounce off the floor, adding turbulence
alternative_answers: Waves reflect off the floor instead of dissipating
Shallow water does not absorb wave energy
headline_answer: Waves bounce off the floor, adding turbulence
source_excerpt: waves... travel downward, bounce off the bottom of the pool, and return to the surface to create turbulence

extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm the Paris 2024 pool was ~2.15m deep and that shallower pools cause waves created by swimmers to bounce off the bottom, increasing turbulence and drag.

explanation: Swimmers generate waves that travel not only sideways but also downward. In a deep pool that energy dissipates in the water column, but a shallow floor reflects it straight back up, so the surface becomes choppier. Swimmers then have to push through more turbulent, wave-filled water, which increases drag and costs fractions of a second. Elite pools are built around 3 metres deep for this reason. The Paris pool was a temporary structure inside a rugby stadium, so its depth was limited, and swimmers and coaches widely blamed it for the slower times.

question: In 1971, astronaut Alan Shepard became the first person to play which sport on the Moon?
source_excerpt: Shepard, using a makeshift club, hit two golf balls on the lunar surface

extra.why_interesting: Players picture astronauts doing science, not sport; the idea that someone packed golf gear to the Moon is delightful and widely half-remembered.
extra.verification_notes: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls with a makeshift 6-iron on the Moon on Feb 6, 1971 during Apollo 14, a well-documented, unambiguous historical fact.

explanation: Shepard smuggled a six-iron head aboard Apollo 14, fixed it to a sample scoop and hit two balls, joking that one went for miles and miles.

question: On a standard six-sided die, the numbers on any two opposite faces always add up to what?
source_excerpt: six is opposite one; five is opposite two; three is opposite four

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has held a die, few have noticed the rule; once heard, it feels obvious and checkable in seconds.
extra.verification_notes: Standard Western dice are manufactured so opposite faces sum to seven (1-6, 2-5, 3-4), a convention dating back centuries with no known exceptions in standard dice.

explanation: One sits opposite six, two opposite five and three opposite four, so every pair of opposite faces totals seven.

question: The puzzle cube invented by architecture professor Ernő Rubik in 1974 came from which country?
source_excerpt: Hungarian inventor, architect and professor of architecture... best known for the invention of mechanical puzzles including the Rubik's Cube

extra.why_interesting: The cube is so global that people rarely place its birthplace; the name sounds vaguely anywhere in Europe, and the Cold War origin surprises.
extra.verification_notes: Ernő Rubik was a Hungarian professor of architecture/design who invented the cube in Budapest, Hungary in 1974.

explanation: Rubik built it in Budapest as a teaching aid for spatial thinking and reportedly took a month to solve his own creation.

question: Which is the only country to have played at every men's football World Cup since the first one in 1930?
source_excerpt: Brazil beat Paraguay 1-0... to secure FIFA World Cup 2026 qualification

extra.why_interesting: Many assume Germany or Italy must share this record, but both have missed tournaments; only one country has a perfect attendance.
extra.verification_notes: Brazil has appeared at all 23 World Cups (1930–2026) and secured its 2026 qualification on June 10, 2025, so the claim remains valid.

explanation: Brazil has never failed to qualify, while heavyweights like Germany, Italy and Argentina have all missed at least one tournament.

question: In which year did IBM's Deep Blue become the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a full match?
source_excerpt: Deep Blue won the six-game rematch 3½–2½...the first defeat of a reigning world champion by a computer under standard chess tournament conditions

extra.why_interesting: People often place this milestone either far earlier, in the 1980s, or much later, in the smartphone era; pinning it to 1997 forces real recall.
extra.verification_notes: Deep Blue defeated reigning world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5–2.5 in May 1997, the first computer to beat a reigning champion under tournament conditions.

explanation: Kasparov won their first match in 1996, then lost the 1997 rematch in New York, a moment often called the end of human supremacy in chess.

question: True or false: an Olympic gold medal is made mostly of silver.
source_excerpt: Olympic gold medals must be made out of at least 92.5% silver... and then they are plated with 6 grams of gold.

extra.why_interesting: The name says gold, so most players assume the medal is gold; in fact it is essentially a silver medal with a thin gold coat.
extra.verification_notes: IOC rules require Olympic gold medals to be at least 92.5% silver, gold-plated with only ~6 grams of gold, so they are indeed made mostly of silver.

explanation: The rules require at least 92.5 percent silver with a plating of about six grams of gold; solid gold medals were last handed out in 1912.

question: Roughly how many tennis balls are used during the two weeks of the Wimbledon Championships each year?
source_excerpt: Wimbledon uses 55,000 tennis balls a year

extra.why_interesting: Players think of a can of balls per match and guess low; the real figure, with balls changed every few games across hundreds of matches, is far bigger.
extra.verification_notes: Wimbledon uses approximately 54,250 tennis balls per year, which falls within the 'tens of thousands' range.

explanation: Around 55,000 balls are used, because new balls come out every seven to nine games across hundreds of matches, and they are stored chilled to keep their bounce consistent.

question: James Naismith's first basketball hoops, nailed to a gym balcony in 1891, were containers originally meant for which fruit?
source_excerpt: He devised 13 original rules and nailed two peach baskets to the gym balcony as the first goals.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the word basketball but never ask what the original baskets were; the answer is charmingly humble and the sport's name suddenly makes literal sense.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm Naismith nailed peach baskets to the gym balcony for the first basketball game in 1891.

explanation: Naismith nailed two peach baskets to the balcony railing, and since they still had bottoms, someone had to fetch the ball out after every score.

question: In snooker, what score is a maximum break, achieved by potting every red with a black and then clearing all the colours?
source_excerpt: A maximum break of 147 points is achieved by potting all 15 reds with 15 blacks for 120 points, followed by all six colours for a further 27 points.

extra.why_interesting: The number is odd and specific, yet a player who knows the point values can reason it out: fifteen reds with blacks, then the colours, and the total lands on a famous figure.
extra.verification_notes: 147 is the correct score for potting all 15 reds with blacks plus clearing the colours; higher scores like O'Sullivan's 153 (2026) require a free-ball scenario, which is a different setup than the one described in the question.

explanation: Fifteen reds paired with fifteen blacks give 120, and the six colours add 27 more, so the perfect frame is worth 147.

question: The marathon's odd distance of 42.195 km was fixed at the 1908 Olympics so the race could start at a royal castle and finish in front of the royal box. Which host city?
source_excerpt: the distance of 26 miles 385 yards (42.195 km)... start within the grounds of Windsor Castle... finish in front of the royal box

extra.why_interesting: People assume the strange distance comes from ancient Greece; in fact it was set to suit a royal family's viewing convenience at one particular Games.
extra.verification_notes: The 1908 Olympics were hosted by London; the marathon started at Windsor Castle and finished in front of the Royal Box at White City Stadium, fixing the distance at 42.195 km, confirmed by Wikipedia and World Athletics.

explanation: The course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium in London, and that awkward length was adopted as the worldwide standard in 1921.

question: Instead of champagne, what drink does the winner of the Indianapolis 500 traditionally down in victory lane?
source_excerpt: Tony Hulman... made the Bottle of Milk a permanent part of the Victory Lane celebration.

extra.why_interesting: Motor racing winners are expected to spray champagne; the idea of a driver gulping milk after 800 km at full speed is an unexpected, endearing image.
extra.verification_notes: The milk tradition dates to 1936/1956 and remains active as of the 2026 race, where winner Felix Rosenqvist drank his pre-selected milk in victory lane.

explanation: The custom began in 1936 when winner Louis Meyer asked for buttermilk, and today drivers even pre-register whether they want whole, two percent or skimmed.

question: The oldest international trophy in sport, first won in 1851 and still contested today, is awarded in which sport?
source_excerpt: The America's Cup was first contested in 1851 making it the oldest trophy in international sport

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for football, cricket or the Olympics, but the oldest trophy still fought over belongs to a sport most would never think of first.
extra.verification_notes: The America's Cup, first contested in 1851, is confirmed as the oldest active trophy in international sport, and it is a sailing competition, still held (37th edition in 2024, 38th planned).

explanation: The America's Cup was first won by the yacht America off the Isle of Wight in 1851, decades before the first modern Olympics or the first football World Cup.

question: Which team event, today mostly seen at school sports days and village fairs, awarded Olympic medals at every Games from 1900 to 1920?
source_excerpt: Tug-of-war was contested as a part of the track & field athletics programme in 1900, 1904, 1906, 1908, 1912, and 1920

extra.why_interesting: The event feels like a school sports day joke, so learning that Olympic medals were once awarded for it is a genuine double-take, yet a thoughtful player can reason toward it.
extra.verification_notes: Tug of war was part of the Olympic athletics programme at every Games held from 1900 to 1920 (1916 was cancelled), confirmed by Wikipedia/Olympedia.

explanation: Teams of eight pulled a rope for Olympic gold, and in 1908 a City of London police team famously won after a dispute about their heavy boots.

question: The leader of the Tour de France wears a yellow jersey. The colour was not chosen for visibility – it was copied from what?
alternative_answers: the newspaper that ran the race
source_excerpt: L'Auto was printed on yellow paper, so organizers decided the race leader's jersey should be yellow too

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the yellow jersey was chosen for visibility in the peloton or as a random tradition; in fact it is a century-old piece of print advertising, matching the yellow newsprint of the newspaper that founded and ran the race.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm the yellow jersey was chosen because L'Auto, the organising newspaper, was printed on yellow paper, introduced in 1919 to make the race leader more visible to spectators.

explanation: The race was founded and run by the sports newspaper L'Auto, which was printed on yellow paper, so the 1919 leader's jersey became a moving advertisement in the same shade.
